newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran faces oil investment showdown with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iran faces oil investment showdown with U.S..

text.p: Iran has reached a critical juncture in its attempts to persuade foreign firms to defy American trade sanctions and invest in Iranian oilfields for the first time since the country's 1979 Islamic revolution.

State National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) is expected next month to award multi-million dollar contracts to international and local firms to develop two offshore fields, Gulf oil industry sources said.
A successful foreign bidder could fall foul of U.S. sanctions aimed at deterring investment in Iran's oil and gas sector.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, citing Tehran as a leading sponsor of international terrorism, signed the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act last August which gave him power to penalise foreign firms that invest $40 million or more a year in either of the two countries' energy sectors.
American oil firms have been banned from buying Iranian oil since 1995.

Leading foreign candidates to get work on the two offshore fields -- known as Soroush and Balal -- are Malaysia's state-owned Petroliam Nasional (Petronas) for Balal and French engineering group Technip, together with an Iranian firm at Soroush, Western oil sources in Tehran said.
Soroush, badly damaged during Iran's 1980-1988 war with Iraq, is planned to produce 90,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil by the year 2000. Balal has potential for 40,000 bpd.
NIOC has not released the names of the final shortlisted firms for the two projects and says that it is comparing the bidders' technical and financial strength.

One known bidder is the government-owned Iranian Offshore Engineering and Construction Company (IOEC) which is already carrying out offshore field work that was originally earmarked for foreign companies.

Industry sources said local firms would get a substantial slice of development work at the fields but added that NIOC was committed to awarding at least some of the work to foreign businesses in an apparent snub to Washington sanctions.
France's Total SA and Elf Aquitaine, Italian Agip SpA and Britain's Premier Oil are amongst others linked to future oil work in Iran but are not seen as front-runners for Balal and Soroush.

"Premier were a leading candidate for Balal but their insistence late in negotiations that they be granted a longer-term management of the developed field hindered its bid," an industry source in the Gulf region said.
Royal Dutch Shell also came close to securing a contract to develop the Sirri fields in 1995 but declined an offer by NIOC who gave the contract to Total.
"It went to a close vote at Shell's board of directors. It was rejected by just one vote -- the chairman's," one source who has been involved in offshore field negotiations said.

Oil industry executives will also be watching for the terms of any awarded contracts on Soroush and Balal following signs that NIOC is showing more flexibility in how firms are financially rewarded for their work.
"Now what is on offer is the opportunity to take crude from Kharg Island and not simply from the field," one Western diplomat based in Tehran said.

Under the original terms of the 11 "buy-back" deals announced in 1995, foreign firms investing in offshore field could only get a return by lifting crude, condensate or gas from the specific project they were awarded.
This had raised concerns amongst some potential bidders that payment could not be guaranteed if the field's reserves were not as large or as productive as initial seismic work suggested.
Total and Petronas so far are the only firms to have invested in Iran's fields and are now actively working to bring onstream Sirri A and E, by the end of this year and 1998 respectively.
Total chairman Thierry Desmarest last month again denied that the threat of U.S. sanctions would deter previous or future Iranian investment by Total.
The French firm is now competing against a consortium led by Shell for the second-phase development of South Pars gas field.

The U.S. State Department's Office of Economic Sanctions Policy will be responsible for implementing the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act but has so far failed to react to energy deals signed by NIOC with Total, Petronas and Turkey.
